facts.text: More big banks are likely to follow, as the rules ease and clients ask for it.
Deutsche Bank gains a fee business and German institutions gain easier access, but Bitcoin and Ether gain buying pressure only if those institutions place orders.
The announcement was made on October 16, 2026, and Deutsche Bank's crypto custody service is set to expand into Asian financial centers in 2027.
If Citi or State Street announces a dated go-live for Bitcoin custody before December 31, the follow-the-leader view gains hard evidence.
In its latest October update, Deutsche Bank has shortened its timeline, saying the launch is now just weeks away and will focus initially on Germany.
Additional services, such as stablecoin offerings, tokenized deposits (which record traditional bank deposits on a blockchain), and digital bonds, will follow, but no specific dates have been set.
Custody banks typically charge a small annual fee, so this business model will be sustainable primarily if clients entrust them with significant assets.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
It became the first of the eight U.S. banks deemed systemically important—banks whose failure could impact the wider economy—to safely hold digital currencies.
Custodians hold assets that clients have already chosen to purchase.
After years of waiting for a good option, SoFi now offers access to major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana, along with more than 25 total digital assets.
What stands out isn't just the selection, it's the integration.
By holding these keys, a bank allows institutions like pension funds or corporate treasuries to own cryptocurrency without needing to handle the keys themselves.
Client demand may also motivate banks to get involved.

The Basel Committee, which develops global bank capital rules, discussed reviewing its crypto regulations in February, suggesting that easing these standards could make it more financially viable for banks to enter the crypto market.

Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst who's spent nearly a decade making blockchain understandable—no easy task when most whitepapers read like fever dreams.
He writes for 24/7 Wall St., covering Bitcoin, altcoins, and crypto market analysis for investors.
Before crypto, he was a tech writer (back when explaining "the cloud" was peak innovation).
Since 2018, he's written for CoinTelegraph, Yahoo Finance, The Block, Cryptonews, Zypto, Rain, and more—basically anywhere people want crypto news without the headache.
Sam runs MacLabs Marketing, a content agency for crypto brands tired of sounding like AI wrote their website.
He also publishes free crypto education on his site for Web3 enthusiasts who think "gas fees" is a typo.
